I have written you a frigging book. I didn't mean to get quite this long winded. I used to be terrified of "pit bulls" until one found me and wouldn't leave until I took him in.

If you want to know the truth of this answer go research on your own. Look at the statistics. Look at the reports filed regarding dog attacks. Talk to respectable dog and animal trainers. Talk to respectable vets. Pay close attention to the "culture" surrounding dog fighting and why they pick the breeds they do. Research the history and origins and decide based on the facts as well as spending some time around them. This is what I did.

So here goes... I have a "pitbull". This is my second one. I have friends who own pit bulls. There really truly isn't any such thing as a "pit bull". Not really. There is the American Staffordshire (AmStaff) Terrier and the American Pit Bull terrier.

There are also people breeding "American Bullies". These are basically pit bull types bred in with other breeds in an attempt to breed some of the small prey drive out of them. They got their start in the 1990s as a "Designer" dog.

There are also all manner of other breeds that also get lumped into or down right confused as being "pit bull type" dog breeds such as the Canne Corso. Block headed labs are sometimes confused as pits by the general public as well.

Then you have the fanatics who breed certain types of "pit bulls" like Gotti line, etc... each line being developed to bring out exact traits. In my area right now "blue nose" pits (bluenose and red nose are not types but descriptive of the colors) are being overbred and inbred due to thug culture and popularity. Certain fighting dog lines can go for thousands and thousands and there is a lot of breeding going on just for looks alone causing behavioral problems in the dogs.

We all know exactly what someone means when they say "pit bull" though. My point is that each dog's individual temperament is going to vary on not just their individual bloodline but how the dog is raised.

If you want to know if the breed is dangerous you have to know a little bit about this "breed" itself. Lots of media friendly and "safe" breeds like the boxer hold very similar origins.

These are traditionally dogs whose ancestors were bred to bait large animals and also to fight for sport. The interesting thing about this is that although it did produce a dog that is very, very game it produced a dog that is also very obedient, easily trainable and easy to handle. Dog fighters or people baiting other large animals had to be able to step into the ring and break up fights (break sticks) and also tend to wounds.

I am absolutely against dog fighting but it's just the history behind many of these breeds, not just "pit bulls".

I do know a man who used to fight dogs and he maintains that the early days of dog fighting almost never ended in death. I haven't researched it that well but it does make sense that anyone investing that much time, energy, effort, and money would throw it away that way. He maintains that it's nigger culture that has resulted in this type of brutality.

I cannot state strongly enough that I detest dog fighting.

I don't know about the fighting side of it in too great detail but irregardless you can't dismiss the violent beginnings of this type of dogs' ancestors. They were bred to be game. They were never bred to be dangerous to humans. Instead loyalty, bravery, and to be easily trainable was bred into them.

Too many people confuse animal aggression with human aggression. A dog that is animal aggressive in no way, shape, form, or fashion means that dog is human aggressive. Any good dog trainer will tell you that.

Although pits are often very animal aggressive they are actually "people pleasers" even to the point of their own detriment. They are willing to fight and die for their owners. The very thing they was actually bred into them - for initially baiting big game animals and later for "sport" - has been twisted and used against them.

The media with all of their hype and scare tactics have been caught in multiple instances of misrepresenting the actual breed(s) involved in an attack. They also rarely report what caused the attacks in the first place. There are several instances of attacks that were actually neighbor dogs getting into a fight and people trying to break it apart. Or... the dog was provoked, the owner threatened, etc...

The perception of these types of breeds has changed over time.

Historically pitbulls were patriotic. The first war dog to receive a medal was Sgt. Stubby, a pitbull. American propaganda from WWII featured pitbulls standing up to German breeds while guarding the American flag and American babies. Circuses used to have performing pit bulls in addition to poodles. Petey on "The Little Rascals" was a pitbull.

Interestingly enough the nickname earned by pit bulls early on was "nanny dog" due to their devotion and loyalty to the children in their families.

Although I would never ever advocate leaving any dog alone with a child unattended my point is that the perception most people have of these types of dogs has drastically changed.

Another interesting fact is that the "dangerous dog breeds" list is constantly changing with what the most popular breeds are at the time. Also there have been numerous cases with misidentified dog breeds in cases of attacks. Many insurance carriers won't write them because they operate off of statistics. You take a very popular group of dogs and combine that with a type of dog that is extremely game and place in a dense area of population and you are going to have problems.

Insurance companies also look at the severity of the risk as well. One attack from a pit or a Rottweiler, etc... is going to result in a much, much expensive claim payout than a dozen toy poodle claims so a lot of the carriers opt out of being put in that situation to begin with.

Pit bulls do not have locking jaws. They do not even have the highest bite pressure over all breeds (Rottweiler if I am remembering correctly). They actually beat out Labrador retrievers and numerous other "safe" breeds on temperament tests. There isn't anything monstrous about them.

Pit bulls actually tend to be extremely friendly "people pleasers" and are very easily trained. They are notorious for going after other animals (which is a big cause of attacks on people, i.e. people who don't or can't control their dogs due to them trying to break up dog fights). My pit though was raised around cats and he gets along great with them. I have seen a lot of videos online showing the same thing from other pit owners.

Honestly it's a combination of genes and upbringing.

Any dog that shows human aggression regardless of breed should be euthanized and never bred. I think they are like any other breed or type of dog. They do better with certain types of people and in certain environments than others.

At the end of the day I would say don't take my word for it. Do your own research and look up the statistics for yourself. Hang out with a pittie or two.

Understand that if you have a pittie a lot of people are going to give you ugly glances, even glares and may say nasty things. I have to take extra precautions when taking my dog out in public. I own multiple breeds and this one is the one that I worry about because he is the friendliest, most trusting, and most outgoing dog I own but often people are trying to start something with him. He likes to bounce, lick, and wiggle with the potential of accidentally knocking a kid over and he is drawn to kids. He lives to play. Which means... I have to be extremely vigilant with him when we are out.

At home he is a champion cuddler and a perpetual wiggle butt. No one can convince me he is anything other than an overgrown toddler trapped in dog form.

And yes, I think if anyone tried to do me harm he would attack. That's really the only situation I believe he would ever attack a human. Despite this let me emphasize the fact that pits are not guard dogs. They do not make good guard dogs. A well bred pit terrier type of dog, is overly friendly with strangers. They will fight to defend if push comes to shove but they had much rather invite a burglar into the house to play than guard their territory.

EDITED to say that I love pit bulls but I absolutely do not agree with the "it's ALL in how you raise them" sentiment. Pits are individuals. They all have differing levels of prey drive but it is still there. You are never going to be able to condition or train a bird dog not to be interested in birds. Bloodhounds will always have their noses pressed up against everything and pit bulls will always have some degree of prey drive. That must be respected. Dogs are not fuzzy children no matter how much we love them.

If you are thinking of getting or taking in a pit bull talk to responsible dog owners who actually OWN the breed. Talk to vets and trainers. Realize that although some pits do and can get along with other dogs or animals in the home most do not.
